findings.claim: D.H. Lawrence's 'A Winter's Tale' is quoted three times as “the mist’s white scarf / Obscures the dark wood and the dull orange sky.” The 4-mark answer key then awards a mark for “the contrast between 'white' (innocence/purity) and 'dark'”.
findings.truth: Lawrence wrote “the mist’s pale scarf”. The word 'white' is not in the poem, so the answer key rewards analysis of a word the student cannot find on the paper. Corrected to 'pale' in the lesson body, the question stem and the answer key (the key's bullet now contrasts 'pale' with 'dark').
findings.evidence: D.H. Lawrence, 'A Winter's Tale', st. 2: 'I cannot see her, since the mist's pale scarf / Obscures the dark wood and the dull orange sky' — https://short-edition.com/en/classic/story/d-h-lawrence/a-winter-s-tale

findings.claim: “In Browning’s ‘The Laboratory,’ the speaker personifies the roses as whispering “Come” in Dunbar-Nelson’s ‘Amid The Roses.’”
findings.truth: The whispering roses belong to Alice Dunbar-Nelson's 'Amid the Roses' alone — st. 2: 'And the still, warm life of the roses fair / That whisper “Come”'. Browning's 'The Laboratory' contains no roses. The sentence credits one poet's image to another poet's poem.
findings.evidence: Alice Dunbar-Nelson, 'Amid the Roses', full text — https://poets.org/poem/amid-roses

findings.claim: “Question 2 is marked out of 8 on three levels. Level 3 (7–8 marks) requires you to ‘identify, explore and compare how the poets use form, language and/or structure’ and ‘compare how the poets use these techniques to affect, manipulate or influence the reader.’” Repeated in the revision tip, the exam tip (“comfortably reach Level 3 (7–8 marks)”) and practice question 6.
findings.truth: The 8-mark unseen comparison is marked across FOUR bands of two marks each (1–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7–8). 7–8 is the TOP band, not band 3. A student told to 'aim for Level 3' would be aiming at 5–6 marks. The two quoted 'requirements' are not the board's wording either; the top band asks for an insightful comparison of the poems and analytical comparison of the effects of the poets' methods. Rewritten in the house band ladder and in house vocabulary, with no descriptor quoted.
findings.evidence: June 2023 mark scheme, 8702/2 Section C Q27.2 [8 marks], AO2 only: Level 4 = 7–8, Level 3 = 5–6, Level 2 = 3–4, Level 1 = 1–2 — https://pmt.physicsandmathstutor.com/download/English-Literature/GCSE/Past-Papers/AQA/Paper-2/MS/June%202023%20MS.pdf

findings.claim: Practice question 5 gives extracts from two poems ('Piano' and 'Yesterday and To-morrow'), asks “Compare the ways the poets present those feelings”, and is labelled “24 marks — Unseen Poetry Analysis” with a 21–24 / 17–20 / 13–16 ... band ladder.
findings.truth: In this section the two-poem comparison is worth 8 marks; the 24-mark question is on a single poem. The label taught students that a comparison answer is a 24-mark task, which would wreck their timing (they would spend 30 minutes on a 15-minute question). Relabelled to the 8-mark comparison and the band ladder rebuilt to the four bands of that question. The alternative fix — replacing the task with a single-poem 24-mark question — would have meant inventing a new mark scheme, so the label was corrected instead.
findings.evidence: Spec §Paper 2 Questions: 'Section C Unseen poetry: Students will answer one question on one unseen poem and one question comparing this poem with a second unseen poem' (specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, line 271); June 2023 MS Q27.1 = 24 marks single poem, Q27.2 = 8 marks comparison.

findings.claim: “Question 2 is worth a third of Section C’s marks”.
findings.truth: The section is 32 marks and question 2 is 8 of them — a quarter, not a third. The lesson states the 32 / 24 / 8 split correctly elsewhere, so this is an arithmetic slip inside a timing warning.
findings.evidence: Spec: Paper 2 = 96 marks; Section C = 24 + 8 = 32 (specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, lines 260, 271–272).

findings.claim: In the 24-mark answer key of lessons 1, 2 and 3 the ladder reads “Top band (21-24) ... Upper band (17-20) ... Top band (13-16) ...” — two different mark ranges both labelled 'Top band'.
findings.truth: 13–16 is the middle band of six, not the top. Relabelled 'Mid band (13-16)' in all three lessons. A student self-marking against this key would read 13/24 as a top-band answer.

findings.claim: Lessons 1, 2 and 4 name the board's attainment levels in student-facing text ('Level 4 (13–16 marks)', 'Level 5', 'Level 6', 'Level 1 (1–2 marks)'), and lesson 1's collapsible reproduces the board's level descriptors close to verbatim ('Convincing, critical analysis...', 'Judicious and precise use of textual references').
findings.truth: The mark ranges themselves are right for the 24-mark question, but 'Level N' is on the house validator's banned list (it rejects the whole unit) and reproducing descriptor wording breaks the copyright-distancing rule. Rewritten to the house ladder (Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic band) and put in plain words.

findings.claim: The exam board is named to students in lesson 1 ('the final section of AQA English Literature Paper 2'; a revision tip about 'the 4 AQA mark scheme rewards'; 'the AQA mark scheme' in practice question 6), lesson 3 ('AQA’s Assessment Objective 2') and lesson 4 ('the AQA comparison mark scheme').
findings.truth: House rule: an exam board's name never appears in student-facing text. Removed in all five places without changing any fact.

findings.claim: “...shows the examiner you understand both AO1 and AO2. Structure comments are rare...”
findings.truth: An AO code immediately followed by a full stop matches the validator's banned spec-code pattern and fails the unit. Rewritten as '...both AO1 and AO2 (methods).' with the meaning unchanged.

findings.claim: The enjambment example says of Yeats “The sentence does not pause at the end of the first line”, quoting 'for peace comes dropping slow, / Dropping from the veils of the morning...'.
findings.truth: That line ends with a comma, so there is a pause — which sits awkwardly beside the lesson's own definition of enjambment as running on 'without a pause'. The sense does run on, so the point is defensible and 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree' offers no comma-free line break to swap in. Left as is; worth a teacher's word in class.
findings.evidence: W.B. Yeats, 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree', st. 2.

findings.claim: Flashcard 5 is 'Name a key concept from ‘Comparing Two Unseen Poems’.' with the answer 'compare' — the same answer as flashcard 1.
findings.truth: A placeholder card, not a factual error: it gives the student a duplicate answer and no new recall. Not edited, because the replacement would be new content rather than a correction.

summary: Every quotation in the unit was checked against a published source and all are verbatim except D.H. Lawrence's 'the mist's pale scarf', misquoted as 'white scarf' in three places including an answer key that rewards the wrong word. The other mark-affecting faults are in lesson 4: the 8-mark comparison is described as having three bands with 7-8 as band 3 (it has four bands and 7-8 is the top), and practice question 5 is a two-poem comparison labelled as a 24-mark single-poem task. Lesson 2 also credits Dunbar-Nelson's whispering roses to Browning's 'The Laboratory'. 28 edits across all four lessons; none is clean.
